seo_title: THT Auto Insertion Line Evaluation for LED Driver Boards: S-3010 Radial + S-70DL Odd-Form | Southern Machinery
seo_desc: Board-by-board evaluation of a THT auto insertion line for an LED driver manufacturer: 1 × S-3010 radial + 3 × S-70DL odd-form, 562–750 boards an hour, cycle per machine, feeder plan and line balance.
seo_keys: THT auto insertion line, LED driver PCB assembly, radial insertion machine, odd-form insertion machine, S-3010, S-70DL, line balance, feeder plan, PCBA evaluation
ans_h2: What line does an LED driver maker need for these four boards?
ans_p: One S-3010 radial inserter plus three S-70DL odd-form inserters build all four LED driver boards at 562 to 750 boards an hour (theoretical, about ±5 % from photos). The radial machine sets the pace on every board; a second S-3010 would lift output to 1,000–1,125 boards an hour.

faq_h2: Questions engineers ask about this line
q1: How accurate is a photo-based evaluation?
a1: About ±5 %. Parts are counted on the board photos; cycle times come from the machine rates used in evaluations. A sample run confirms the figures, and the equipment PO specification prevails.
q2: Why does the radial machine set the line speed?
a2: Each board carries more radial parts than one S-3010 can insert in the time three S-70DL machines need for the odd-form parts, so the odd-form cells wait for the radial cell.
q3: What would a second S-3010 change?
a3: In this concept view the radial cycle halves, and line output rises to 1,000 boards an hour on boards 1, 2 and 4 and 1,125 on board 3.
q4: Which radial parts can the S-3010 insert?
a4: Taped radial parts up to 20 mm body height and 10 mm diameter, with 2.5, 5.0, 7.5 or 10.0 mm lead spans, unwinding at no more than 5 N.
q5: How fast is the S-70DL on heavy parts?
a5: It averages 0.9 s per part; transformers and large connectors take 0.9 to 1.3 s each, which the estimate already includes.
q6: What do you need from us for a firm proposal?
a6: Sample panels and parts, the BOM with packaging per part, and your shift pattern. We return a timed sample-run video, a line layout and a quotation.

bl1t: Why LED driver boards still eat hand-insertion hours
bl1s: Where the hours go on a through-hole driver board, and how to see it on your own line.
bl1p1: Walk past a hand-insertion line on an LED driver board and you will see the same picture every shift: twenty people, hundreds of parts each, and a supervisor counting boards against the plan.
bl1p2: The pain is not the people. It is that every driver board carries a mix of radial capacitors and heavy odd-form parts, so no single machine looked like the answer, and hand insertion stayed by default.
bl1p3: Split the problem in two. Count the taped radial parts and the odd-form parts on each board, then give each group its own machine type. In our evaluation the four boards carried 12 to 16 radial and 8 to 12 odd-form parts each.
bl1p4: That split is exactly how the proposed line is built: one S-3010 for the radial parts and three S-70DL cells for transformers, connectors and terminals, reaching 562 to 750 boards an hour on paper.
bl1p5: Re-count every new board the same way. When the radial share grows, you will know before the line slows down.
bl1p6: Send us photos of your boards and we will mark every part and return the same board-by-board figures.
bl2t: Count your parts before you buy a machine
bl2s: A photo, two colours of marker and a simple rule give a first line plan in days.
bl2p1: Most machine quotes start with a brochure. A better start is a photo of your panel.
bl2p2: Buyers often get a machine speed in components per hour and no idea what it means for their own board, so the decision drags on.
bl2p3: Mark every through-hole part on the photo: red circles for taped radial parts, blue boxes for odd-form parts. Multiply by boards per panel, divide by the machine rate, and you have a cycle per panel.
bl2p4: Our evaluation applies that method board by board. The S-3010 is rated at about 9,000 parts an hour and each S-70DL at about 4,000, both including PCB transfer and mark recognition.
bl2p5: Keep the marked photo with the board's documents. Every engineering change becomes a quick re-count instead of a new study.
bl2p6: Email your panel photos; we return the marked photos and the cycle table within the week.
bl3t: Radial or odd-form: which parts go where
bl3s: A practical way to split an LED driver BOM between two machine types.
bl3p1: Every driver board has two personalities: rows of small taped capacitors and a handful of bulky parts that refuse to sit on a tape.
bl3p2: Trying to run both on one machine either slows the radial parts or leaves the heavy parts by hand.
bl3p3: Send taped radial parts within 20 mm body height and 10 mm diameter to the radial inserter. Send transformers, connectors, terminals and large capacitors to an odd-form inserter fed by tube, tray, bulk or tape feeders.
bl3p4: In this line the S-3010 handles spans of 2.5, 5.0, 7.5 and 10.0 mm, and the S-70DL places odd-form parts in 0.9 s on average, 0.9 to 1.3 s for heavy ones.
bl3p5: Review the split whenever a supplier changes packaging; a part that moves from tape to bulk changes which feeder it needs.
bl3p6: Share your BOM with packaging per part and we will return the split for your boards.
bl4t: Find the machine that sets your line speed
bl4s: Line output is decided by one machine. Here is how to find it.
bl4p1: A line is only as fast as its slowest machine, yet most plans add up machine speeds as if they ran alone.
bl4p2: The result is a line that looks fast on paper and waits all day in practice.
bl4p3: Work out the cycle per panel for each machine group, take the slowest one, and divide 3,600 seconds by it. Multiply by boards per panel for boards an hour.
bl4p4: On these four boards the S-3010 takes 19.2 to 38.4 s per panel while the three S-70DL cells need 14.4 to 18.0 s, so the radial machine sets the pace every time.
bl4p5: Re-run the check for each new board; the bottleneck can move when the part mix changes.
bl4p6: Ask us for the line balance table for your boards.
bl5t: Planning feeders for transformers, connectors and terminals
bl5s: How odd-form parts are spread over three stations.
bl5p1: Odd-form automation fails less on the machine than on the feeders.
bl5p2: Parts arrive in tubes, trays, bulk bags and tape, and a plan that ignores packaging stalls at the first changeover.
bl5p3: Group odd-form parts by packaging, then spread the groups over the stations so each station carries a similar load: bulk and tape on one, tubes on the next, tray parts where the tray feeder fits.
bl5p4: The plan for these boards uses three S-70DL stations, FS#1 to FS#3, with tube, tray, bulk and tape feeders shown per board in the feeder table.
bl5p5: Freeze the plan only after the BOM confirms packaging, and keep it with the program for each board.
bl5p6: Send packaging details per part and we will draft the feeder plan for your boards.
bl6t: Getting radial parts ready for automatic insertion
bl6s: The checks that keep a radial inserter running.
bl6p1: A radial inserter stops more often for bad tape than for anything inside the machine.
bl6p2: Parts on loose or over-tight tape, or with bodies too tall, turn a fast machine into a slow one.
bl6p3: Check three things before the first run: body height and diameter, lead span, and the force needed to unwind the tape.
bl6p4: For the S-3010 that means bodies up to 20 mm high and 10 mm in diameter, spans of 2.5 to 10.0 mm, and a pull-out force of no more than 5 N.
bl6p5: Add these checks to incoming inspection so every new lot is ready for the machine.
bl6p6: Download the readiness checklist from the catalogues on this page, or ask us to review your parts.
bl7t: When a second radial inserter makes sense
bl7s: Reading the line balance figures before adding a machine.
bl7p1: If one machine sets the pace, the fastest way to more output is often a second one of the same kind.
bl7p2: Adding capacity in the wrong place buys machines that wait.
bl7p3: Compare the bottleneck cycle with the next slowest group. If the gap is large, doubling the bottleneck moves the whole line.
bl7p4: In this concept view a second S-3010 lifts output from 750 to 1,000 boards an hour on boards 1 and 2, from 562 to 1,000 on board 4 and from 562 to 1,125 on board 3.
bl7p5: Check the balance again whenever volumes or boards change; the right line today may differ next year.
bl7p6: Ask us for the line layout and quotation for both options.
bl8t: From sample panels to a running THT line
bl8s: A step-by-step path from evaluation to production.
bl8p1: A good evaluation is the first step, not the last.
bl8p2: Teams lose months between a promising estimate and a running line because nobody owns the steps in between.
bl8p3: Follow four steps: photo evaluation, sample run on the real machines, line layout for your floor, then a formal quotation with feeders, programming, installation and training.
bl8p4: This report covers step one for four LED driver boards; the sample run turns the ±5 % estimate into measured cycle times.
bl8p5: Keep the same board figures through every step so each decision builds on the last.
bl8p6: Send sample panels and parts to start the sample run.
